paragraphs: Continual learning systems can retain a small collection of earlier examples and replay them while learning new tasks. Choosing this collection, or coreset, requires deciding which examples will support useful model training. The paper argues that existing approaches either use expensive greedy searches over discrete choices or simplify away the nested relationship between selecting data and training a model.

The proposed formulation learns a probability distribution over examples. Its inner optimization trains a model to minimize expected error under that distribution. Its outer optimization adjusts the distribution so that the resulting model performs well on the full dataset. A regularizer based on a smoothed top-K loss encourages approximately K nonzero probabilities, linking the distribution to the desired memory size.

The authors provide an algorithm with a convergence guarantee to an approximate stationary point and a stated computational complexity. Experiments cover balanced data, imbalanced data, and label noise, reporting substantial improvements over competitive baselines. The algorithm also reduces running time relative to vanilla greedy selection on continual learning benchmarks. These results support preserving the nested optimization structure while replacing direct discrete search.
neurips-2023-bilevel-coreset-selection-i.tldr: A new bilevel formulation selects replay examples through sparse sampling probabilities, improving continual learning results and runtime in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: This paper develops a mathematical framework for building deep learning models with kernels. Its starting point is the reproducing kernel Hilbert C*-module, or RKHM, which extends the familiar reproducing kernel Hilbert space using C*-algebra. The authors combine this structure with the Perron-Frobenius operator, a linear operator connected to composing functions, to describe a framework called deep RKHM.

The central contribution is theoretical: the authors derive a new Rademacher generalization bound and use Perron-Frobenius operators to interpret benign overfitting. The bound describes generalization within this framework, and its dependence on output dimension is milder than that of existing bounds. This gives a more favorable theoretical treatment of output dimensionality, rather than establishing an unconditional guarantee of better predictive performance.

The algebraic formulation also exposes the product structure of operators and provides a connection to convolutional neural networks. Together, these results offer tools for reasoning about how layered kernel models are constructed and how they generalize. The paper’s stated value is a new perspective for designing and analyzing deep kernel methods, grounded in a shared operator-based mathematical language.
neurips-2023-deep-learning-with-kernels-.tldr: Deep RKHM combines generalized kernel spaces and composition operators to analyze deep kernel models, including generalization and benign overfitting.

paragraphs: Two images can resemble one another in object pose, composition, and meaning even when their local colors or textures differ. This paper argues that existing perceptual similarity metrics miss important aspects of that broader resemblance. It introduces DreamSim, a metric trained to bring image comparisons into closer agreement with human visual judgments.

The authors first use text-to-image models to generate synthetic image pairs that differ along varied visual dimensions. They collect human similarity judgments on these pairs, aiming for comparisons that people make readily and consistently. Existing metrics struggle to explain this dataset, so the authors tune a new metric using the judgments. Their analysis finds that DreamSim emphasizes foreground objects and semantic content while remaining sensitive to color and layout.

Although its training data are synthetic, DreamSim transfers to real images in the reported retrieval and reconstruction tasks. It outperforms previous learned metrics and recent large vision models on those tasks. The findings show that deliberately generated comparisons can provide useful supervision for a more holistic similarity measure, with benefits extending beyond the synthetic images used to train it.
neurips-2023-dreamsim-learning-new-dimen.tldr: DreamSim learns from human judgments of synthetic image pairs to measure broader visual similarity and transfers successfully to real-image tasks.

paragraphs: An explanation of a Gaussian process prediction can carry uncertainty, just as the prediction itself does. This paper develops a way to retain that uncertainty when assigning contributions to input features. It extends Shapley values to stochastic cooperative games, producing explanations that are random variables and can use the Gaussian process’s full analytical covariance structure.

The resulting explanations satisfy axioms similar to the favorable properties of ordinary Shapley values. They also have a tractable covariance function spanning both features and observations. This means the framework can describe uncertainty in individual contributions and statistical relationships among explanations. The explanation is therefore richer than a collection of separate feature scores: it can represent how those scores vary together.

The authors also address predictive explanation, where explanations for new data are estimated from previously computed ones. They introduce a Shapley prior over the explanation function to support that prediction. Extensive illustrations demonstrate the approach’s effectiveness. The contribution is a unified treatment of feature attribution, uncertainty, and dependence for Gaussian processes, together with a way to extend computed explanations to additional observations.
neurips-2023-explaining-the-uncertain-st.tldr: Stochastic Shapley values explain Gaussian processes while retaining uncertainty and dependencies between feature contributions.

paragraphs: Relative entropy coding communicates a sample from a target distribution using a proposal distribution while seeking a short bit representation. It can accommodate continuous distributions without quantization, making it relevant to learned compression and differentially private federated learning. However, slow execution and restrictive assumptions have hindered its use. The paper introduces Greedy Rejection Coding, or GRC, to address these obstacles.

GRC generalizes an earlier rejection-sampling approach to arbitrary probability spaces and partitioning schemes. The authors prove that it terminates almost surely and produces unbiased target samples. For continuous distributions on the real line with a unimodal target-to-proposal density ratio, the GRCS variant has optimal expected code length and a runtime bound proportional to KL divergence, with a multiplicative constant of approximately 4.82.

For GRCD, another variant, stronger runtime and code-length bounds are supported experimentally and conjectured under the same assumptions; they are not presented as established theorems. The authors also test GRC in a variational-autoencoder compression pipeline on MNIST. A modified training objective and an additional code-length compression method further improve efficiency, connecting the coding analysis to a working compression application.
neurips-2023-faster-relative-entropy-cod.tldr: Greedy Rejection Coding improves relative entropy coding, with optimal-runtime guarantees for one variant under specific distributional assumptions.

paragraphs: Real-world graphs contain varied structures and different kinds of nodes and edges. A graph neural network must accommodate this diversity while remaining trainable and computationally manageable. This paper introduces Graph Mixture of Experts, or GMoE, to increase a model’s ability to adapt to different graph structures without an explosive increase in computational overhead.

GMoE lets individual nodes dynamically select experts that aggregate information. Different experts learn to handle distinct subgroups of graph structures and gather information over different hop distances. Experts with larger hop sizes specialize in collecting information from farther away. The design makes the choice of how to gather graph information adaptive at the node level, giving the model several specialized aggregation options.

The authors evaluate GMoE on graph, node, and link prediction tasks from the OGB benchmark. They report effectiveness across these tasks, including ROC-AUC improvements of 1.81% on ogbg-molhiv and 1.40% on ogbg-molbbbp relative to non-MoE baselines. These findings support explicit expert specialization as a practical way to handle structural diversity in the evaluated graph learning settings.
neurips-2023-graph-mixture-of-experts-le.tldr: GMoE lets graph nodes select specialized aggregation experts, improving performance across the reported graph learning tasks.

paragraphs: Transferring knowledge between graphs is difficult because both node attributes and graph structure can change. A model learned on a source graph therefore faces a distribution shift when applied to a related target graph. This paper introduces GraphGP, a graph-structured Gaussian process framework designed to adaptively transfer knowledge across such graph domains.

The framework accommodates either homophily or heterophily assumptions, allowing it to address graphs with different patterns of connection between nodes. GraphGP is derived from a new neural network that accounts for graph structure, by taking a limit in which its layers become infinitely wide. This construction connects the proposed graph neural architecture to a Gaussian process formulation for transfer learning.

The authors’ generalization analysis explicitly examines how transferability relates to similarity between graph domains. Their experiments on several transferable graph learning benchmarks show that GraphGP is effective relative to state-of-the-art Gaussian process baselines. Together, the analysis and experiments tie the transfer problem to both node information and structural relationships, providing a framework for studying when related graphs support useful knowledge transfer.
neurips-2023-graph-structured-gaussian-p.tldr: GraphGP derives a graph-aware Gaussian process for knowledge transfer and analyzes how transferability relates to similarity between graph domains.

paragraphs: Learning useful representations of people requires attention to body structure. This paper introduces masked image modeling as a pre-training approach for human-centric perception, then adapts it using prior knowledge about human parts. The resulting method, HAP, changes how image regions are hidden during training so that the learning process gives greater emphasis to human structure.

Patches corresponding to human body parts receive higher priority for masking. This encourages the model to concentrate on structural information during pre-training. HAP also includes an alignment loss that brings representations of different masked views of the same image closer together. Because those views are guided by human parts, the loss is intended to capture human characteristics that remain consistent across different masking patterns.

Using a plain vision transformer encoder, HAP achieves new state-of-the-art results on 11 human-centric benchmarks and comparable performance on one further dataset. The evaluated tasks include person re-identification, pedestrian attribute recognition, and estimation of human pose and shape. The breadth of these reported gains supports the usefulness of incorporating body-part structure into pre-training across several forms of human perception.
neurips-2023-hap-structure-aware-masked-.tldr: HAP uses body-part-guided masking and view alignment to improve pre-training for multiple human perception tasks.

paragraphs: Prompts provide a way to control generative models, but finding useful wording often depends on manual experimentation. This paper focuses on hard prompts: actual words and tokens that can be supplied through a text interface. It contrasts them with soft prompts, which are continuous feature vectors amenable to optimization but harder to edit, reuse across models, or enter as text.

The authors propose an efficient gradient-based method for automatically optimizing hard text prompts. The approach applies to both text-to-image and text-only applications. Its practical aim is to make prompt discovery accessible without requiring users to know in advance how to phrase the desired request. For image applications, the authors describe generating, discovering, and combining concepts through the optimized prompts.

The paper also reports bypassing Midjourney’s token-level content filters by optimizing through an openly available text encoder. This is a stated finding about that filtering setup, alongside the method’s prompt-tuning applications. Overall, the contribution brings gradient-based optimization to discrete text prompts while retaining a form that users can work with through ordinary text interfaces.
neurips-2023-hard-prompts-made-easy-grad.tldr: The paper introduces gradient-based optimization of hard text prompts for text and image generation, and reports a token-filter bypass application.

paragraphs: A neural network can place similar images near one another without organizing its entire representation space in a useful way. This paper investigates whether human similarity judgments can improve that broader organization. The authors focus on linearly aligning neural representations with human judgments, asking how the overall geometry affects subsequent learning tasks.

Their initial approach reveals a tradeoff: naive alignment changes local relationships substantially and harms downstream performance. The proposed global-local transform addresses this by aligning the global structure while preserving local structure. In practical terms, the method seeks to improve the arrangement of the representation space without losing the useful neighborhood relationships that the original network already learned.

The resulting transform considerably improves accuracy across a variety of few-shot learning and anomaly detection tasks. The findings indicate that the global organization of human visual representations can support learning from few examples, and that incorporating this organization benefits neural representations in the evaluated tasks. The paper therefore identifies both a useful source of supervision and a reason that applying it without local preservation can fail.
neurips-2023-improving-neural-network-re.tldr: Aligning global neural representation structure with human similarity judgments improves downstream tasks when local relationships are preserved.

paragraphs: Neural reinforcement learning agents can learn policies with limited prior structure, but understanding their behavior is difficult, especially when they work from images. Neuro-symbolic approaches seek policies whose structure is interpretable. This paper emphasizes that interpretability alone does not establish explainability and introduces NUDGE with the aim of achieving both properties.

NUDGE uses trained neural agents to guide the search for candidate logic rules with associated weights. It then trains logic-based agents using differentiable logic. The neural agents thus provide guidance during the search, while the resulting policy is expressed through logical rules. This connects the capabilities of trained neural policies to a policy form intended to support understanding and explanation of behavior.

In the reported experiments, NUDGE produces interpretable and explainable policies while outperforming purely neural agents. The authors also report flexibility across environments with different initial states and problem sizes. These findings support the approach in the tested settings: neural guidance can help discover logical policies that combine readable decision structure with strong task performance and adaptation to environmental variations.
neurips-2023-interpretable-and-explainab.tldr: NUDGE uses neural agents to guide the discovery of trainable logical policies that are interpretable, explainable, and effective in reported experiments.

paragraphs: A weak learner only needs to classify better than random by some margin under the relevant data distribution. Boosting builds on such learners as components of a larger model. This paper explores whether prompt-based language models can fill that role for tabular data, expanding their use beyond directly answering a few-shot classification prompt.

The method supplies the language model with text descriptions of tabular examples sampled appropriately for the distribution of interest. The model produces a summary that acts as a classification template. These templates serve as weak learners within a boosting approach. Sampling is central to the construction because the language model must produce a useful classifier for the particular distribution presented to it.

The authors find that the resulting approach can use knowledge within the language model to outperform traditional tree-based boosting in many settings. It also surpasses few-shot learning and occasionally more involved fine-tuning procedures, particularly on some tasks with small datasets. These results demonstrate a practical role for language models as components of broader learning algorithms, without establishing that every prompted model satisfies weak-learning guarantees universally.
neurips-2023-language-models-are-weak-le.tldr: Prompted language models can supply weak classifiers for boosting on tabular data, with strong results in several settings involving limited data.

paragraphs: Mesogeos is a dataset designed to support several kinds of wildfire modeling in the Mediterranean. It brings together weather, vegetation, and human-activity variables with historical wildfire ignitions and burned areas. The records cover 17 years, from 2006 through 2022, providing a shared basis for studying wildfire drivers alongside recorded fire events.

The authors harmonize these variables into a cloud-friendly datacube with one-kilometer spatial cells and daily time steps. This common spatial and temporal structure makes the variables available within the same organized dataset. From it, they extract two machine-learning-ready tracks: forecasting short-term wildfire danger and estimating the final burned area given an ignition point. These tracks address different prediction questions using the shared resource.

The paper defines evaluation metrics and baseline models for both tracks. It also releases the datacube and code for constructing the machine learning datasets and models. The contribution is therefore both a data resource and an evaluation starting point. Its multipurpose design is intended to support additional wildfire modeling tasks beyond the two tracks demonstrated in the paper.
neurips-2023-mesogeos-a-multi-purpose-da.tldr: Mesogeos harmonizes Mediterranean wildfire drivers and fire records into a daily spatial dataset with two machine learning evaluation tracks.

paragraphs: When formalizing mathematics with a proof assistant, finding relevant existing knowledge is an important task. MLFMF provides datasets for benchmarking recommendation systems that help identify useful theorems, constructions, datatypes, and postulates. The collection draws on Lean’s Mathlib and several large Agda libraries, giving learning systems access to substantial bodies of formalized mathematics.

Each library is represented in two complementary forms. A heterogeneous network records its modular organization and references between entries. A collection of s-expressions represents the syntax trees of individual entries, preserving their complete contents in an easily parsed format. Together, these forms expose both how mathematical entries relate to one another and how each entry is structured internally.

The authors report baseline results using graph and word embeddings, tree ensembles, and instance-based learning. With more than 250,000 entries, they describe MLFMF as the largest collection of formalized mathematical knowledge in machine-learnable form at the time of the work. The extraction methodology can extend to other libraries and proof assistants, making the contribution a reusable benchmarking approach as well as a specific dataset collection.
neurips-2023-mlfmf-data-sets-for-machine.tldr: MLFMF turns large formal mathematics libraries into graph and syntax datasets for benchmarking recommendations of relevant mathematical knowledge.

paragraphs: Streaming estimation becomes difficult when the quantity being tracked changes and the incoming data contain heavy-tailed noise or arbitrary corruptions. This paper studies these difficulties together for estimation problems with strongly convex losses. It proves that an appropriately tuned clipped stochastic gradient descent method can adapt to drift, tolerate both kinds of contamination, and operate online without distributional knowledge.

The learning rate must balance responsiveness against noise. The authors explain that neither the usual inverse-time rate for stationary strongly convex problems nor the constant rate suited to noiseless drift provides the required balance. They instead use a rate based on the stream length raised to a negative power, with an exponent below one. A doubling strategy removes the need to know the stream length beforehand.

The analysis combines a new inductive argument with martingale concentration to obtain high-probability results across learning rates under arbitrary distribution shifts. The authors present this as the first online estimation algorithm with simultaneous guarantees for heavy tails, corruptions, and distribution shift. Synthetic and real-data experiments complement the theory, whose strong-convexity requirement and tuning conditions are integral to the stated result.
neurips-2023-online-robust-non-stationar.tldr: Appropriately tuned clipped SGD provides simultaneous robustness to drift, heavy tails, and corruptions for strongly convex online estimation.

paragraphs: When a neural filtering model outperforms a Kalman filter, the difference may reflect how the models were optimized as well as their architectures. This paper identifies a comparison problem in nonlinear filtering: neural models are often optimized, while the reference linear Kalman filter is left unoptimized. That makes it difficult to separate the value of nonlinear architecture from the value of parameter fitting.

The authors introduce the Optimized Kalman Filter, or OKF, to make the optimization treatment more comparable. Their results show that a Kalman filter may become competitive with neural models when optimized using OKF. This supports their criticism of conclusions in certain earlier studies: an observed gap under unequal optimization does not cleanly establish the advantage of the neural architecture.

The paper examines OKF’s advantage over the standard Kalman filter through both theoretical and empirical work across a variety of problems. It also highlights a practical benefit: existing systems can replace their standard filter with OKF by updating parameters. The contribution therefore concerns both fairer experimental evaluation and a potentially useful improvement to an established filtering method.
neurips-2023-optimization-or-architectur.tldr: Optimizing Kalman filter parameters can make the filter competitive with neural models and exposes confounded comparisons between optimization and architecture.

paragraphs: Related datasets may share useful features while also containing patterns specific to each dataset. Personalized Dictionary Learning, or PerDL, formalizes the problem of learning sparse linear representations that preserve both kinds of information. It represents common features with a global dictionary and dataset-specific features with local dictionaries, while treating their separation as something to learn.

The challenge extends beyond ordinary dictionary learning because the shared and unique components are initially unknown. The authors establish conditions under which the global and local dictionaries can be provably disentangled. They then introduce Personalized Matching and Averaging, or PerMA, a meta-algorithm that recovers both dictionary types under these conditions. Its convergence to the ground truth is linear under suitable assumptions.

PerMA also lets stronger learners improve the predictions of weaker learners by sharing useful information. The paper illustrates PerDL in tasks including training with imbalanced datasets and video surveillance. The framework’s significance is its explicit handling of commonality and individuality, backed by conditional recovery guarantees rather than an assumption that every heterogeneous collection can automatically be separated correctly.
neurips-2023-personalized-dictionary-lea.tldr: PerDL separates shared and dataset-specific sparse representations, with a recovery algorithm that converges linearly under suitable conditions.

paragraphs: POP-3D aims to turn two-dimensional images into a three-dimensional map that can be queried with free-form language. The map represents occupied space using voxels, or three-dimensional cells, and associates them with language embeddings. The task is difficult because images do not uniquely specify three-dimensional structure, and manual language annotations for three-dimensional scenes are hard to obtain.

The architecture combines a 2D-to-3D encoder with separate occupancy and 3D-language heads. Its dense output supports locating, segmenting, and retrieving scene content through language. To train it, the authors develop a self-supervised method combining images, language, and LiDAR point clouds. A strong pretrained vision-language model supplies supervision without requiring manually created 3D language annotations.

The paper evaluates zero-shot 3D semantic segmentation on existing datasets, along with grounding and retrieval for free-form language queries. For the latter tasks, it introduces a small extension of nuScenes. The reported quantitative results demonstrate the model’s strengths across these tasks. The approach connects image-based 3D occupancy prediction to language-compatible representations, while using LiDAR as part of its multimodal training procedure.
neurips-2023-pop-3d-open-vocabulary-3d-o.tldr: POP-3D predicts language-queryable 3D occupancy maps from images using multimodal training without manual 3D language annotations.

paragraphs: Object-centric learning represents a scene through a collection of object entities called slots. These structured representations offer possibilities for controlled generation and object manipulation, but existing slot-based methods can decode them into blurry images or distorted objects. SlotDiffusion addresses this bottleneck by focusing on how object representations are converted back into visual content.

The method is an object-centric latent diffusion model for images and videos. It uses the modeling capacity of latent diffusion to improve slot-to-image decoding. Across six datasets, the authors report better unsupervised object segmentation and visual generation than previous slot models. The results link stronger visual decoding with improvements in both generated output and the discovery of objects.

The learned object features can also be used by existing object-centric dynamics models, improving video prediction and downstream temporal reasoning in the reported evaluations. When combined with self-supervised pretrained image encoders, SlotDiffusion also scales to unconstrained real-world datasets such as PASCAL VOC and COCO. This integration condition matters: the stated real-world scalability is demonstrated with those pretrained encoders as part of the system.
neurips-2023-slotdiffusion-object-centri.tldr: SlotDiffusion improves object-based image and video modeling with latent diffusion, benefiting segmentation, generation, and temporal tasks.

paragraphs: Some neural network explanation methods use the Hessian to study interactions between input features. This creates a problem for ReLU networks: their piecewise-linear structure gives them a zero Hessian almost everywhere. SmoothHess addresses this obstacle by examining a smoothed version of the network, allowing second-order interactions to be estimated through a different mathematical route.

The method estimates the Hessian after the network function has been convolved with a Gaussian. Using Stein’s lemma, it turns this task into an efficient sampling procedure that requires only network gradient calls. Users can explicitly control the extent of smoothing. The method is applied after training and requires no change to the ReLU architecture, making the target of explanation a controllably smoothed network function.

The authors provide a non-asymptotic sample-complexity bound for the estimation procedure. They also validate its superior ability to capture interactions on benchmark datasets and a medical spirometry dataset. These results support Gaussian smoothing as a way to recover useful interaction information when the original network’s almost-everywhere-zero Hessian prevents a direct second-order analysis.
neurips-2023-smoothhess-relu-network-fea.tldr: SmoothHess estimates feature interactions in Gaussian-smoothed ReLU networks using gradient samples and Stein’s lemma.

paragraphs: Dataset distillation seeks small synthetic datasets that preserve essential information from much larger collections. This paper focuses on how those synthetic datasets are represented, arguing that their parameterization is important for efficiency and performance. The proposed SPEED framework uses dictionary learning and sparse coding to construct compact epitomes containing pivotal dataset information.

SPEED captures spatial redundancy both within individual synthetic images and across them. Spatial-Agnostic Epitomic Tokens and Sparse Coding Matrices provide mechanisms for representing and selecting significant features. A Feature-Recurrent Network generates hierarchical features with high compression and storage efficiency. Together, these components address the representation of the distilled data, allowing shared visual information to be handled compactly.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks and downstream applications, with particular strength on high-resolution datasets. SPEED is also compatible with several dataset matching approaches and generally improves their performance. The findings suggest that better synthetic-data parameterization can complement existing matching methods: gains can come from changing how distilled information is stored and generated, alongside the criteria used to match the original dataset.
neurips-2023-sparse-parameterization-for.tldr: SPEED uses sparse coding and compact hierarchical features to improve dataset distillation, especially for high-resolution data.

paragraphs: Generating a panorama from multiple diffusion windows requires more than hiding the seams between images. Even when overlapping latent features are averaged, the result can combine incompatible scenes into one montage. SyncDiffusion addresses this broader coherence problem by synchronizing the diffusion processes through a perceptual similarity objective.

At each denoising step, the method uses predicted denoised images to compute a perceptual loss and its gradient. Gradient descent then provides guidance for coordinating the multiple diffusions. The authors present this as a plug-and-play module, allowing coherence guidance to be added to a generation process. Using predicted clean images gives the similarity objective meaningful visual content throughout denoising.

The reported user study favors SyncDiffusion’s coherence over previous methods by 66.35% to 33.65%. The authors also report maintaining image fidelity and compatibility with the input prompt, assessed using GIQA and CLIP score. Demonstrations cover layout-guided generation, conditional generation, and 360-degree panoramas. These results support perceptual synchronization as a way to improve agreement across generated regions while preserving other evaluated aspects of image quality.
neurips-2023-syncdiffusion-coherent-mont.tldr: SyncDiffusion coordinates multiple diffusion windows through perceptual gradients to produce more coherent panoramas and image montages.

paragraphs: Observational data often leave several causal structures compatible with what has been measured. Interventions can help distinguish among them, but acquiring intervention data can require substantial time, money, or physical resources. This paper studies how to target those interventions so that causal discovery can proceed with fewer required experiments.

The proposed method, Gradient-based Intervention Targeting, or GIT, draws its targeting signals from the gradient estimator of a gradient-based causal discovery framework. It uses information from that framework to guide which intervention data to acquire. This connects experimental selection to the procedure already being used to infer causal structure, making the gradient estimator part of the data-acquisition strategy.

The authors evaluate GIT extensively on simulated and real-world datasets. They report performance comparable to competitive baselines overall and better performance in the low-data regime. That qualification is central to the finding: the clearest reported advantage occurs when data are scarce. The results support gradient-guided intervention selection as a useful approach for allocating expensive experiments, particularly when the available evidence is limited.
neurips-2023-trust-your-nabla-gradient-b.tldr: GIT uses causal-discovery gradients to target interventions, matching competitive methods overall and surpassing them when data are scarce.

paragraphs: White blood cell image datasets often identify cell categories without describing the visible characteristics behind those categories. WBCAtt adds detailed morphological annotations to support more interpretable recognition models. The paper focuses on the appearance of cells and their components, providing information that connects image-based recognition to features examined in pathology.

The authors identify 11 attributes through collaboration with pathologists, a literature review, and manual inspection of microscopic images. These attributes describe the cell, nucleus, cytoplasm, and granules. They annotate approximately 10,300 images, producing about 113,000 labels. This gives the dataset a level of descriptive detail beyond a single category label for each cell and supplies explicit targets for learning morphological attributes.

The paper includes experiments that predict these attributes from cell images and demonstrates applications that benefit from the annotations. Its contribution is a resource for investigating how white blood cell recognition models relate to visible morphology. The stated findings support attribute prediction and explanation-oriented applications, with the broader aim of advancing explainable artificial intelligence in pathology and hematology.
neurips-2023-wbcatt-a-white-blood-cell-d.tldr: WBCAtt adds 11 morphological attributes to roughly 10,300 white blood cell images to support interpretable recognition and attribute prediction.

paragraphs: Fast visual trackers often reduce input size, sacrificing information that could improve tracking accuracy. ZoomTrack changes how a cropped image is resized so that a small input retains more detail where the target is likely to appear. The aim is to preserve a broad visual field while allocating more of the available resolution to the likely target region.

The resizing is nonuniform: regions with higher target likelihood receive higher resolution, while other regions receive less. The authors formulate this operation as a quadratic programming problem that can be solved efficiently. It can be integrated into most crop-based local trackers, making input preparation the central mechanism for improving the speed–accuracy tradeoff.

Experiments on five datasets using OSTrack and TransT show consistent improvements. On TNL2K, the modified speed-oriented OSTrack exceeds its performance-oriented counterpart by 0.6% AUC while running 50% faster and using over 55% fewer multiply-accumulate operations. This specific result illustrates the paper’s broader finding that target-aware resizing can narrow, and in some evaluated cases close, the accuracy gap associated with smaller tracker inputs.
neurips-2023-zoomtrack-target-aware-non-.tldr: ZoomTrack preserves detail near likely target locations through nonuniform resizing, improving the accuracy of fast visual trackers.
